notes:
Two notes before the commentary:

- **What I didn't find:** I found nothing for Psalm 129 from netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org, catholic.com, oca.org, the Lutheran or Pentecostal sites, or any prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching. Those are left out.
- **Protestant traditions don't really split on this psalm.** Calvin (Reformed), Gill and Spurgeon (Baptist), Benson (Methodist) and Guzik (Calvary Chapel) agree on the basic meaning. They differ only in what they stress, and I've marked those differences below. The Catholic voices are Augustine and Bellarmine. Augustine's Psalms numbering runs one behind (he calls this Psalm 128).

**v. 1**
- **Israel's "youth" (traditional reading):** Ellicott says "youth" means the start of the nation's life, reaching back to slavery in Egypt. Here, of course, not the youth of a person, but of the nation. The poet glances back even to the Egyptian bondage. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/129-1.htm
- **On "now":** Ellicott points out that the Hebrew has no adverb of time, so it simply means "let Israel say." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/129-1.htm
- **Calvin (Reformed):** the psalm was probably written at a time when the Church of God, reduced to a state of extreme distress... was on the verge of total destruction. For him "youth" also covers the hard lives of Abraham and the patriarchs. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/129-1.html
- **Gill (Baptist) reads the verse on several levels:**
  - literal Israel;
  - the church, persecuted by pagan Rome and then by Rome Papal;
  - each believer, whose "youth" is their conversion;
  - and even the Messiah, one of whose names is Israel.
  https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/hnv/psalms/129-1.html and https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/bsb/psalms/129-1.html
- **Guzik (enduringword):** he applies the verse to the Jewish people, who have outlasted wave after wave of persecution from Egypt to the Nazis. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-129/
- **Clarke:** the psalm was written after the captivity (the exile in Babylon). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/129-1.html

**v. 2**
- **Spurgeon (Baptist):** saying it twice is poetry, a way to make a sonnet out of her sorrows, music out of her miseries. The enemy had many chances but not so much as once has he gained the victory. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/129-1.htm
- **Keil & Delitzsch:** this verse is the turning point. The Hebrew word here carries the sense "nevertheless." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/129-1.htm
- **Augustine (Catholic):** enemies attack the good because they could not prevail upon me, meaning the good man consents not with him to evil. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801129.htm

**v. 3**
- **What the picture means.** Most see it as whipping that leaves marks like furrows:
  - Spurgeon: The scourgers tore the flesh as ploughmen furrow a field. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps129.cfm
  - Jamieson-Fausset-Brown agree, and Barnes thinks the psalmist probably had Israel's slavery in Egypt in mind. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/129-3.htm
- **Others say it is general oppression, not literal whipping:**
  - Calvin takes it as a picture of the church as a field; for him, the cross has always been planted on the back of the Church. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/129-3.html
  - Ingram Cobbin (quoted by Spurgeon) sees no need to look for an interpretation of this in scourging. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps129.cfm
- **Clarke's alternative:** the people may have been yoked to the plough, made to pull it like animals. He says Jerome read it this way. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/psalms-129.html
- **The Hebrew word for "furrows":** Delitzsch says it means the strip of land ploughed at one time. Either way, the point is that they did their cruel work thoroughly and spared nothing. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/129-3.htm
- **Pointing to Christ:**
  - Benson (Methodist) links it to Isaiah 50:6, where the Servant gives his back to those who beat him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/129-3.htm
  - Samuel Eyles Pierce (quoted by Spurgeon) sees it fulfilled when Jesus was flogged. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps129.cfm
- **God's purpose in the ploughing:**
  - Alexander Henderson (Scottish Presbyterian): God controls the "plough" of persecution and uses it to prepare his people to receive his word.
  - Jeremy Taylor (Anglican): God fails not to sow blessings in the furrows.
  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps129.cfm
- **Ancient translations:** the Septuagint (the old Greek translation) reads The sinners wrought upon my back. https://biblehub.com/psalms/129-3.htm Augustine follows this kind of text: Upon my back have sinners built. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801129.htm

**v. 4**
- **Spurgeon:** this verse is the hinge of the condition. God cuts the rope that ties the oxen to the plough. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps129.cfm
- **Matthew Henry:** God cut the harness, the whips, the ties that held the enemies together, and the bonds of captivity. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/129-2.html
- **Constable:** the cords may be the plowman's reins, or simply whatever held Israel bound. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/129-3.html
- **Guzik:** "the LORD is righteous" means God keeps his promises to Israel. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-129/
- **Benson:** God defeated the enemies' plans using the very means they meant to use to destroy the church. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/129-3.htm
- **Augustine (Catholic):** his text says the Lord will hew the necks of the sinners. He takes the "neck" to mean proud sinners who will not admit their sins. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801129.htm
- **Past or future?** bible.org notes that the verb could be read as a wish ("Let YHWH cut the cords"), but Most English translations... translate the verb as a past event. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-129

**v. 5**
- **Prayer or prediction?**
  - The Cambridge Bible finds it hard to decide, but leans toward reading it as an expression of faith that the enemies will fail.
  - The Pulpit Commentary allows either a wish or a confident expectation.
  - Barnes reads it as a prayer.
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/129-5.htm
- **Defending the prayer against enemies (an "imprecation"):**
  - Spurgeon: If this be an imprecation, let it stand. A note he quotes adds that the psalmist says "all who hate Zion," not "all who hate me," so the motive is zeal for God's people, not revenge. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps129.cfm
  - Boice (quoted by Guzik) finds these curses remarkably mild. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-129/
- **Bellarmine (Catholic):** the words can be read as a wish for a "good confusion" that leads enemies to repent and turn to God. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps129.cfm
- **Who "Zion" means:**
  - bible.org: national Israel, centred on the temple. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-129
  - Gill: the people of the church, its King, and the gospel. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nkj/psalms/129-5.html
  - Cambridge Bible: the historical haters were people like Sanballat and Tobiah, who opposed rebuilding Jerusalem in Nehemiah's day. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/129-5.htm

**v. 6**
- **The picture:** flat roofs grew grass that had no depth of soil and withered quickly. Maclaren says it shows the short-lived success and rapid extinction of plots against Zion. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/psalms-129.html
- **Calvin:** don't be afraid of proud enemies. Like roof grass, they sit high but have no root, it being humility alone which draws life and vigor from God. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/129-5.html
- **A translation question.** Some read "before it grows up," others "before it is plucked up":
  - Barnes says the second is what the Hebrew means, and that the Septuagint, the Latin Vulgate and Luther render it that way.
  - Cambridge calls it possible but less suitable.
  - Ellicott thinks the clause probably contains a textual error.
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/129-6.htm
- **Augustine:** the roof grass is seen on high, and has not a root. It withers even before God's judgment comes. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801129.htm
- **Spurgeon's notes:** they compare these enemies to the stony-ground hearers in Jesus' parable of the sower. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps129.cfm

**v. 7**
- **Matthew Henry:** their attacks on Zion will never ripen, and they will gain no more from them than a farmer gains from grass on his roof. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/129-5.html
- **Coffman:** This stands for total worthlessness. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/129-8.html
- **Augustine:** he links the verse to the final harvest, when reapers gather the wheat and bind the tares (weeds) for burning. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801129.htm

**v. 8**
- **The custom:** passers-by greeted reapers with a blessing, as in Ruth 2:4 (Pulpit Commentary, Barnes). Barnes calls the verse language drawn from common life, a prayer that Zion's enemies would not succeed. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/129-8.htm
- **Who speaks the second line?** Gill and Cambridge say "we bless you" may continue the passer-by's greeting or be the reapers' reply, as the Targum (an old Aramaic paraphrase) takes it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/129-8.html and https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/129-8.htm
- **Matthew Henry:** wishing enemies success in their plans against the church means sharing in their evil (2 John 11). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/129-8.html
- **Augustine:** the "passers-by" are the prophets and apostles. They blessed those with the root of love but gave no blessing to the proud. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801129.htm
